```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The committed files that the build writes
panel <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
measures <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
by_edu <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_edu.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about the work between a download and a model: reading the raw files of a survey, selecting the respondents or the events that a study analyses, recoding the answers into the variables that its paper describes, building the measures that the models need, turning the data into the unit on which the model is fitted, and checking the result against a target that you did not compute yourself. The [three-day course](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/day-2.qmd) builds the analysis file of the case from the raw files in the second session of day 2, after downloading those files on day 1 by the routes that the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) sets out, and this module is the reading for that session. The self-study track takes the build in [stage 10](../tracks/self-study/stage-10.qmd), and the one-day course on data tools reads its outline in [Part 3](../tracks/eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/part-3.qmd).

Section 1 sets out the steps that every build shares. Section 2 takes them in turn, with the code that does them, for the country-year panel of the EU-frames paper from sixteen Eurobarometer waves, and section 3 draws out the habits that carry over to a project of your own. The module assumes the [R module](intro-r.qmd).

The code of the build is taken from the preparation scripts of the workspace and from the pipeline of the case, the numbered scripts in `R/eu-frames/` that write its data files, rearranged as a sequence of steps that you can run one at a time in your IDE. Code that reads a raw or licensed file is shown and not run on this page, which is built without those files; what each step produces is shown from the files that the course committed, which the same steps wrote. The second script of the workspace was run on the respondent file on 27 October 2026 and printed the comparison that section 2.7 quotes. The build ends with a comparison of your file with the committed one, so that a rebuild on your own machine either reproduces the file of the course or says where it differs.

## 1. The steps of a build {#sec-steps}

Whatever the survey, a build from raw files goes through the same six steps, in this order.

1. **Read** the raw files, with their labels where they have them (Stata and SPSS files carry the wording of each question and answer) or by the column positions that a setup file gives where they have none (fixed-width text).
2. **Select** the rows that the study analyses: its countries, rounds or waves, respondents and events, by the rules that the paper states.
3. **Recode** the answers into the variables that the paper describes: reversed scales, groups, indicators that take the value 0 or 1, dates, and the codes for refusals and non-answers turned into missing values.
4. **Derive** the measures that the models need and that no single question gives: a scale built from several items, the length of a union, the party in government on the day of an interview.
5. **Reshape or aggregate** the rows into the unit on which the model is fitted: one row per respondent, one row per month in which an event could happen, one row per country and year.
6. **Check** the result against a target: the counts of the paper, the file of the course, the checksum of a file.

Three rules hold throughout. The raw files stay in a folder outside the workspace and are never edited; every change is made by the code, so that a reader can see it. The code meets the raw files in one place, a folder named at the top of the script, so that someone else can point the same code at their own copy. And files derived from licensed microdata go into a folder that git ignores, from the first day.

| | EU frames |
|---|---|
| Raw files | Sixteen Eurobarometer waves in Stata format |
| Unit of the analysis file | Country-year |
| Size | `r nrow(panel)` country-years from `r format(sum(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents |
| Target of the check | The committed panel, to the precision of floating-point arithmetic |
| Code in the course | `prep/01_build_respondents.R` and `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` in the workspace |
| Who may receive the result | The panel, anyone; the respondent file, nobody |

: The build at a glance.

## 2. The country-year panel from the Eurobarometer {#sec-eu-frames}

The original author (OA) of the EU-frames case [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] scored the answers of the respondents of sixteen Eurobarometer waves to the question on what the European Union means to them into four framing scales, and modelled them within their countries and waves, with two economic series merged by country and year. The course panel, `EUframes_cy.csv`, averages the same respondents into 270 country-years, as analyst C6HJR did in Multi100, and every page of the one-day courses starts from it. The three-day course builds it from the raw waves with two scripts of the workspace: `prep/01_build_respondents.R`, which you run once, and `prep/02_scales_and_panel.R`, which you read and run step by step. The first rebuilds the respondent file of the course from your own GESIS downloads and checks the result against the course build. The second rebuilds the country-year panel that is distributed with the course, to machine precision, and then builds the panel by education band on which the individual-level extension is based. The pipeline of the case does the same work for the curve of the claim in `R/eu-frames/01_person_file.R` and `07_measurement_panels.R`, and `15_analyst_panels.R` builds, from the same waves, the panels of two of the five analysts, following the code that each deposited.

If you have not downloaded the sixteen files, everything here can still be read, because what the scripts print is quoted on the page; nothing that reads the respondent file can be run.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Licensed microdata {#the-file-you-are-about-to-build-is-licensed-microdata}

The GESIS terms of use apply to everything that the first script writes. The respondent file stays in `data_private/`, which is kept out of version control by the `.gitignore` file in the workspace. It is never uploaded, shared, or opened in a session that an AI assistant can read, because the terms prohibit processing the data with AI systems. It is deleted when the project ends. The aggregates distributed with the course are subject to none of these restrictions, and the second script shows where the line between the two falls.
:::

### 2.1 The respondent file {#sec-build}

`prep/01_build_respondents.R` is written to be run as a whole: set the folder that holds the sixteen files at the top, then source the script. It does five things, and it prints a report at the end.

**It checks the files.** The script contains an inventory of the sixteen studies: the file name under which GESIS serves each study, the study number, the wave, the year to which the course assigns the wave, where the battery of the question starts, the column of the design weight, and the MD5 checksum of the file from which the course panel was built. The first rows read:

```{r}
#| label: eu-inventory
#| eval: false
inventory <- tibble::tribble(
  ~file,               ~study,   ~eb,    ~year, ~cntry_v,   ~items_from, ~items_style, ~w1_v, ~md5,
  "ZA4056_v1-0-1.dta", "ZA4056", "61.0", 2004, "isocntry",  63,  "v",    "v9", "0fc7763a1b0ae4bac6fb70bf87d07543",
  "ZA4229_v1-1-0.dta", "ZA4229", "62.0", 2004, "v7",        105, "v",    "v8", "76051b80553ee29be104d13777eeae31",
  "ZA5689_v2-0-0.dta", "ZA5689", "79.3", 2013, "isocntry",  0,   "qa14", "w1", "e46f479d0d82b4d0cc3fccd69b708397"
)
```

A missing file stops the script with the study number to fetch. The two studies that GESIS serves zipped, ZA4506 and ZA4744, are unpacked beside their archives. The checksum of every file is compared with the inventory, and the report says, file by file, whether yours is byte for byte identical to the one that the course used. The comparison makes the rest of the course reproducible on your own machine. If the sixteen checksums match, every number on this site can be rebuilt from your folder.

**It finds the question in each file.** The battery on what the EU means occupies sixteen adjacent columns in every file, fourteen items followed by "other" and "don't know", but the position of those columns differs. In the twelve older files the columns are numbered (`v63` to `v78` in EB 61.0, `v105` onwards in EB 62.0) and in the four newest they are named after the question (`qa12_1` to `qa12_16` in EB 76.3). The inventory records the start of the block or the question stem for each wave, and the script reads the sixteen columns by that rule and checks that every value is 0 or 1. The respondent characteristics are found differently, by their variable labels rather than their positions, because the occupation item in particular moves from wave to wave. If a label pattern matches two variables, the script stops instead of picking one.

**It harmonises Germany and the United Kingdom**, which the survey samples as two regions each, into one country each, and keeps the twenty-seven member states of the period.

**It codes the respondent characteristics as the published models code them.** Sex as a female indicator. Education as the age at which full-time schooling finished, with the two codings that the [individual-level exercise](individual-level.qmd) offers: the published three bands, which replace "still studying" with the current age of the respondent and cut at 16 and 20, and a four-band version that keeps the students as a band of their own. Occupation collapsed into the eight groups of the published models, with the unemployed as their own group. Urbanisation in three categories. Left–right placement on its ten-point scale, missing in the four waves that did not ask it. The step is one call of `dplyr::mutate()` on the stacked waves:

```{r}
#| label: eu-characteristics
#| eval: false
respondents <- respondents |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    female  = as.integer(gender == 2),
    edu_raw = edu,
    edu4    = dplyr::case_when(edu_raw == 98            ~ "studying",
                               edu_raw %in% c(97, 0:15) ~ "le15",
                               edu_raw %in% 16:19       ~ "e16_19",
                               edu_raw %in% 20:96       ~ "e20plus",
                               TRUE                     ~ NA_character_),
    edu     = dplyr::if_else(edu %in% c(0, 97, 99), NA_real_, edu),
    edu     = dplyr::if_else(edu == 98, age, edu),
    edu3    = dplyr::case_when(edu < 16              ~ "low",
                               edu >= 16 & edu <= 19 ~ "mid",
                               edu > 19              ~ "high",
                               TRUE                  ~ NA_character_),
    ses     = dplyr::case_when(occ %in% 5:9   ~ "self_employed",
                               occ %in% 10:12 ~ "manager",
                               occ %in% 13:14 ~ "white_collar",
                               occ %in% 15:18 ~ "manual",
                               occ == 1       ~ "house_person",
                               occ == 3       ~ "unemployed",
                               occ == 4       ~ "retired",
                               occ == 2       ~ "student",
                               TRUE           ~ NA_character_),
    unemployed = as.integer(ses == "unemployed"),
    urban   = dplyr::case_when(urban == 1 ~ "rural", urban == 2 ~ "small_town",
                               urban == 3 ~ "large_town", TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    rile    = dplyr::if_else(rile %in% 1:10, rile, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(exclude = c("gender", "occ"))
```

**It compares the result with the course files.** The number of respondents in every country-year is checked against the committed panel, and the counts of respondents who named none of the thirteen items, split into those who said "don't know", those who gave another answer and those who left the question blank, are checked against the committed cell file. When the checksums match, all 270 cells match on both counts. On a folder holding the sixteen files that the course used, the printed report looks like this:

```
 study  eb   year rows_eu27 identical_to_course_file
 ZA4056 61.0 2004 16216     TRUE
 ZA4229 62.0 2004 26807     TRUE
 ...
 ZA5689 79.3 2013 26605     TRUE

 check                                                           value
 files found                                                      16
 files identical to the course build                              16
 country-years in the committed panel                            270
 country-years rebuilt                                           270
 cells with an identical respondent count                        270
 cells with identical no-opinion counts (none, DK, other, blank) 270

Every check passed: your file is the one from which the course panel was built.
```

The respondent file then holds `r format(sum(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` rows and 31 columns, the respondents of the 270 country-years.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the script and read the report. Then open `data_private/build_report.csv` and find the wave with the fewest respondents. It is the spring 2004 wave, fielded before the ten accession states joined; every later wave has about twenty-six and a half thousand respondents in the twenty-seven states.
:::

### 2.2 Which items form which scale {#sec-items}

`prep/02_scales_and_panel.R` is written to be read from the top and run a section at a time. It makes the measurement decisions of the course explicit one at a time, in the order in which the pipeline needs them. The published paper assigns the thirteen scored items to four scales, cosmopolitan, utilitarian, communitarian and libertarian, and the course adds the positive and the negative composite. The script states the assignment as four vectors of item names, since at this point a scale is no more than a list:

```{r}
#| label: eu-items
#| eval: false
items <- list(
  cosmo = paste0("it", c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7)),  # peace, democracy, travel, diversity, say
  util  = paste0("it", c(2, 4)),           # prosperity, social protection
  comm  = paste0("it", c(9, 12, 13, 14)),  # unemployment, identity, crime, frontiers
  lib   = paste0("it", c(10, 11))          # bureaucracy, waste of money
)
items <- c(items, list(pos = c(items$cosmo, items$util), neg = c(items$comm, items$lib)))
items13 <- c(items$pos, items$neg)
```

The euro item (`it8`) is kept in the respondent file and never scored, as in the paper. The [measurement module](measurement.qmd) tests whether the data agree with the assignment.

### 2.3 Three scoring rules {#sec-scoring}

The answers of a respondent to a set of items can become one number in more than one way, and the full menu of the course offers three: the share, which is the published rule and divides the mentions of items in the set by the total of the respondent; the count, which is the number of items in the set that were mentioned; and the per-item rate, which divides the count by the number of items in the set. The script computes all three for every scale, side by side, from the same item columns, adding a count (`c_`), a share (`s_`) and a rate (`r_`) for one scale at a time with `purrr::reduce()`:

```{r}
#| label: eu-scoring
#| eval: false
scored <- names(items) |>
  purrr::reduce(\(d, s) {
    d |>
      dplyr::mutate("c_{s}" := datawizard::row_sums(dplyr::pick(dplyr::all_of(items[[s]]))),
                    "s_{s}" := dplyr::if_else(n_all == 0, 0, .data[[paste0("c_", s)]] / n_all),
                    "r_{s}" := .data[[paste0("c_", s)]] / length(items[[s]]))
  }, .init = dplyr::mutate(respondents,
                           n_all = datawizard::row_sums(dplyr::pick(dplyr::all_of(items13)))))
```

The share is compositional, meaning that the four scales sum to one for anyone who mentioned anything. The count measures how many items were mentioned, and its four scales have no such constraint. That is why the specification menu treats the rule as a decision about what the outcome is rather than about how it is measured, and the curve of the claim keeps only the share, for the reasons that the [measurement module](measurement.qmd#sec-count) gives.

### 2.4 The respondent who named nothing {#sec-noop}

About six per cent of respondents mentioned none of the thirteen items, and a share has no denominator for them. The code of the original study drops them, since a division by a total of zero leaves them missing, while the course panel scores them zero on every scale, and the script does the same (the `if_else()` above); the curve of the claim keeps both rules. The [missing-answers module](missingness.qmd) sets out the alternatives, which are dropping them, splitting them across the scales, or imputing them. The first script keeps the "don't know", "other" and blank codes apart because the three groups are different people, and treating them alike is itself a decision.

### 2.5 From respondents to country-years {#sec-aggregate}

The course panel averages every respondent in a country-year with the same weight, which the course calls 'as interviewed'. The post-stratification weight that GESIS supplies with each file, which corrects a national sample to its population, is the other choice, and the script computes both means so that the two can be compared in the [weights module](weighting.qmd). It also records the count of respondents in each cell, which is used by a precision weight at the next stage.

```{r}
#| label: eu-aggregate
#| eval: false
cells <- scored |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("s_"), mean, .names = "m{.col}"),
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("s_"), \(x) stats::weighted.mean(x, w1), .names = "w{.col}"),
    dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("c_"), mean, .names = "m{.col}"),
    n_cy = dplyr::n(),
    .by = c(cntry, year)
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^ms_", "m", x), dplyr::starts_with("ms_")) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^ws_", "w_m", x), dplyr::starts_with("ws_")) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sub("^mc_", "c_m", x), dplyr::starts_with("mc_"))
```

This is the step at which the licensed microdata become an aggregate that may be shared: from here on, every row is a country-year, and the smallest mean in the panel rests on `r format(min(panel$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents.

### 2.6 The macro series {#sec-merge}

The unemployment rate and the growth series join the panel by country and year. The script merges them from the file that contains every series offered by the menu, `predictor_measures.csv`, which is distributed with the course so that the merge works offline; the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) shows the call of the `WDI` package that fetches the same World Bank indicators live. A live fetch can differ in the last decimals because the Bank revises past years, so the course records which release of each series it used. This step reads only committed files, so this page runs it and compares the result with the two columns of the panel:

```{r}
#| label: eu-merge
macro <- measures |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure %in% c("wb_nat", "wb_growth")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "year", "predictor", "value")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = predictor, values_from = value)

panel |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("cntry", "year", "unemp", "growth")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(macro, by = c("cntry", "year"), suffix = c("_panel", "_merged")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rows = dplyr::n(),
                   unemp = max(abs(unemp_panel - unemp_merged)),
                   growth = max(abs(growth_panel - growth_merged)))
```

The two series agree with the panel exactly in all 270 country-years. The bailout indicator is not merged from any file. It is coded by rule from the record of assistance programmes, and the codebook states the rule.

### 2.7 Does it reproduce the panel? {#sec-reproduce}

The rebuilt panel is compared column by column with the panel distributed with the course. On the file from which the course was built, the six as-interviewed scale means, the respondent counts and the two macro series agree to machine precision, and so do the design-weighted and the count-built means in the cell file:

```
 column max_abs_difference
 mcosmo 5.551115e-17
 mutil  2.775558e-17
 mcomm  5.551115e-17
 mlib   2.775558e-17
 mpos   5.551115e-17
 mneg   5.551115e-17
 n_cy   0.000000e+00
 unemp  0.000000e+00
 growth 0.000000e+00
```

A difference of five parts in a hundred million billion is the rounding of floating-point arithmetic, not a difference in the data.

A reproducible data pipeline, in the sense used in this course, is one in which anyone with the same sixteen files and this script gets the same 270 rows, and can alter any decision above and find out what changes in the panel.

### 2.8 The panel by education band {#sec-edu}

The last section of the script builds a second panel, one row per country, year and education band, with the same six scales and the number of respondents behind each mean. It is the aggregate used in the individual-level extension of the course to ask whether unemployment narrows the gap between the high- and the low-educated. Unlike the respondent file, it can be committed and shared, because a cell mean over at least `r min(by_edu$n)` people, and in half of the cells more than `r floor(stats::median(by_edu$n))`, reveals nothing about any of them. Its `r format(nrow(by_edu), big.mark = ",")` rows are `cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_edu.csv`, and the rebuild reproduces them to machine precision.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the scoring rule in section 2.3 from the share to the count for the cosmopolitan scale, re-run the aggregation and the comparison, and read the column of differences. The as-interviewed cosmopolitan mean now differs from the course panel in every cell, and the count-built column of the cell file agrees instead. Then change the no-opinion rule so that respondents who named nothing are dropped rather than scored zero, and read the respondent counts. Each is a one-line change in the script and a decision on the specification menu.
:::

## 3. Beyond the case {#sec-beyond}

The six steps of section 1 recur in most survey work, and the build of section 2 shows them in one of their shapes, many waves aggregated into a panel. The [section of the R module on other formats](intro-r.qmd#sec-formats) has the functions for the file formats, and the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) the routes by which the raw files arrive. Three habits from this build apply to any project. Keep an inventory of the files that you read, with their versions and checksums, in the script itself, so that the data on which a result rests are stated where the result is computed. Check every build against a target that you did not compute, a count printed in the paper or a file that someone else built, and write the check into the script so that it runs every time. And keep the licensed and the shareable in different folders from the first day, with the ignore rule written before the first file is downloaded.
